This is open, and cannot be resolved with a finite computation.
Let $\alpha>1$ be irrational. Are there infinitely many primes $p$ such that $\lfloor p\alpha\rfloor$ is also prime?
#972: [Er65b]
number theory
Vinogradov [Vi48] proved that the sequence $\{p\alpha\}$ is uniformly distributed for every irrational $\alpha$, and hence there are infinitely many primes $p$ of the shape $p=\lfloor n\alpha\rfloor$ for every irrational $\alpha>1$. Indeed, this occurs if and only if\[\frac{p}{\alpha}\leq n<\frac{p+1}{\alpha},\]which is true if and only if $\{p\alpha^{-1}\}>1-\alpha^{-1}$, which happens infinitely often by the uniform distribution of $\{p\alpha^{-1}\}$.

 The result should be true for every $\alpha \in \mathbb R^+ \setminus \mathbb N$.
For $\alpha = 1/2$, it is e.g. equivalent with the existence of infinitely many Sophie Germain primes, for which one guess there are $2C(1+o(1)) \frac{x}{\ln^2 x}$ many up to $x$. 
Here $C$ is Hardy–Littlewood's twin prime constant (somewhat confirming the connection).
In general, one indeed expects for fixed valid $\alpha$ ($\alpha \in \mathbb N$ are excluded for obvious reasons, where $\alpha=1$ is trivially a special case) the number of valid primes indeed to be of the order $\frac{x}{\ln^2 x}$.
